title: A comprehensive review on the potential application of coal mine drainage sludge as a resource in ecological environment
abstract: Abstract Large volumes of coal mine drainage sludge (CMDS), a byproduct of acid mine drainage (AMD) treatment, impose both environmental and operational burdens. This review comprehensively evaluates the potential of CMDS as a sustainable resource and introduces a novel integrated framework covering its formation mechanisms, physicochemical properties, environmental risks, and application pathways. Rich in iron, aluminum, and manganese oxides, CMDS features a high specific surface area and porosity, making it suitable for use as an adsorbent. Pretreated CMDS can adsorb arsenic at capacities reaching 67 mg g − 1 , with strong desorption and reusability. When applied as an iron source in Fenton-like oxidation, it achieves up to 98% chemical oxygen demand and total organic carbon removal. In combination with calcium-based wastes, it significantly reduces As, Cu, and Pb leaching by more than 90% in soil. Nevertheless, concerns over secondary metal release persist. This study discusses these limitations and proposes a “dual-core” strategy integrating AMD treatment optimization with targeted CMDS modification, offering a new direction for ecological remediation and circular resource utilization in mining-impacted areas.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Abundant coal mine drainage sludge (CMDS) is generated due to active and passive AMD remediation. Global data from 108 mining sites revealed that each site annually produced an average of approximately 9.5 kt of dry sludge, with outputs ranging from 0.02 to 135 kt, and that the sludge volume, depending on its solid content, varied by a factor of approximately 2 to 70 times its dry mass [ 10 ]. CMDS management involves dewatering, stabilization, transport, and dredging, which incurs costs between 23 and $75 t − 1 , accounting for 5–20% of the operational costs of AMD treatment systems [ 10 ,  11 ]. The release and migration of metals/metalloids such as Fe, Al, Mn, Cd, Zn, and As from CMDS [ 12 ,  13 – 14 ] pose significant environmental concerns. Most treatment systems fail to achieve their anticipated lifespan due to the production and accumulation of CMDS [ 15 ,  16 – 17 ]. Notably, these CMDS are often enriched with substantial amounts of heavy metals derived from AMD, including Fe, Mn, As, and Cd. If not properly managed, they may continuously release secondary pollutants, thereby degrading surrounding ecosystems and posing serious threats to human health [ 18 ,  19 ]. Thus, traditional AMD treatment technologies are costlier, due to which innovative, cost effective, and environmentally benign methods for managing CMDS are being investigated [ 11 ,  20 ,  21 ].

CMDS, owing to its high iron content, is considered a valuable resource for various applications. However, the properties of CMDS produced using different AMD treatment technologies and sludge management approaches vary considerably; therefore, the same type of CMDS have diverse suitability for specific applications. Therefore, a systematic review on the resource utilization of CMDS remains lacking, particularly one that offers a comprehensive evaluation framework encompassing the full chain from formation mechanisms, physicochemical heterogeneity, and environmental risks to utilization pathways and performance optimization. To address this research gap, this study systematically reviews how different AMD treatment strategies influence the composition and structure of CMDS, and summarizes its application pathways in various fields, including heavy metal adsorption, organic wastewater treatment, soil stabilization, and rare earth pollution remediation. Furthermore, the coupling relationship between its resource potential and environmental risks is explored, and an AMD treatment optimization strategy centered on resource recovery is proposed. This work aims to provide both theoretical support and technical reference for transforming CMDS from an environmental burden into a sustainable resource. Its novelty lies in the establishment of a performance optimization framework oriented towards CMDS applications, and a thorough analysis of the feasibility and key constraints of its high-value utilization. The study ultimately advocates for a shift in AMD management toward a “dual-core” model that simultaneously optimizes effluent quality and CMDS quality, offering significant scientific value and practical application potential.

sections.heading: Active treatment
paragraphs: The impact of active AMD treatment methodologies such as neutralization, electrochemical, membrane-based, biological processes, and ion exchange on the properties of the resultant CMDS was investigated [ 17 ]. Results revealed that CMDS derived from neutralization and electrochemical processes demonstrated higher solids content and lower reagent consumption, improving practical reuse value.

sections.heading: Neutralization
paragraphs: Neutralization is primarily categorized into high-density sludge (HDS) and low-density sludge (LDS) methods [ 22 ]. The LDS method treats AMD by adjusting its pH, enhancing oxygenation via aeration, and employing flocculation and sedimentation. Due to slow reaction kinetics, the resulting sludge is rich in alkaline substances and generates CMDS with a solids content of < 5% [ 23 ]. In contrast, the HDS method produces CMDS with a higher solids content, typically ranging from 20 to 40%. Through internal recirculation of CMDS to the pH adjustment tank, the process enhances sludge solids concentration, promotes the aggregation of ferric hydroxide particles, and significantly accelerates their settling. These improvements result in up to 50% smaller clarifier volumes, 30% lower lime consumption, and a 75% reduction in site footprint, which collectively improve dewatering efficiency and substantially reduce both capital costs and carbon footprint [ 24 ]. The LDS method is predominantly employed for AMD treatment due to its ease of regulation. CMDS produced using LDS and HDS methods are similar, with particle sizes ranging from 2.9 to 42.5 μm [ 12 ,  13 ,  25 ]. It is primarily composed of amorphous/crystalline Fe and Al oxides/hydroxides (e.g., goethite, hematite, lepidocrocite, and magnetite) as well as gypsum and calcite [ 12 ,  25 ,  26 – 27 ].

The neutralization process that elevates the pH above 11, also known as ettringite precipitation [ 28 ], forms ettringite, a hydrated calcium aluminum sulfate hydroxide (Ca 6 Al 2 [(OH) 12 |(SO 4 ) 3 ]·26H 2 O). A key advantage of ettringite is its ability to incorporate “undesirable” ions into the Ca 2+ , Al 3+ , OH − , and SO 4 2−  lattice structure via coprecipitation; it thus removes sulfates and aluminum along with contaminants such as Cr, As, and Cd [ 29 ]. This principle underpins the development of the SAVMIN™ process [ 30 ,  31 ], which enables the production of gypsum, and calcite from AMD. To date, due to relatively high plant and maintenance costs, this process has been implemented only at a few locations in South Africa [ 17 ]. Thus, CMDS produced via ettringite precipitation has not been discussed herein.

sections.heading: Electrochemical process
paragraphs: Herein electrocoagulation is primarily discussed, and electrosorption (capacitive deionization) and electrodialysis have not been discussed due to their limited operational facility.

Compared to neutralization, electrocoagulation can considerably reduce operational costs and recover high-purity metals from mine waters. It is widely applied for AMD treatment at multiple sites [ 32 ,  33 – 34 ]. However, electrocoagulation systems are susceptible to electrode fouling and inter-electrode clogging, resulting from the rapid precipitation and deposition of metal oxides and hydroxides, which form coal mine drainage sludge (CMDS) [ 35 ]. Consequently, frequent CMDS removal is required to maintain stable electrochemical performance and hydraulic functionality.

Electrocoagulation does not require the addition of other cationic agents and operates at low pH; it predominantly yields CMDS composed of iron oxides and hydroxides (α-FeOOH) that typically constitute > 90% of the composition along with heavy metals from the AMD [ 36 ,  37 – 38 ].

sections.heading: Membrane treatment process
paragraphs: Membrane treatment processes, including microfiltration, nanofiltration, ultrafiltration, and reverse osmosis, have limited applicability due to their high membrane scaling and the associated damages. Seed precipitation reverse osmosis (SPARRO) has been employed to address this issue, in which gypsum crystals are used as seed nuclei [ 30 ,  39 ,  40 ,  41 ,  42 ,  43 – 44 ]. However, pilot trials have demonstrated that SPARRO that does not involve mine water pretreatment is economically viable only to a limited extent [ 45 ]. Therefore, this process is primarily employed in the advanced treatment stage before reusing mine wastewater (in conjunction with other treatment processes). The composition of CMDS adhered to membranes—mainly influenced by the pretreatment process, as the membrane separation does not alter the precipitate properties—is beyond the scope of this discussion.

sections.heading: Biological process
paragraphs: Biological processes are categorized into active and passive approaches. A notable example is the THIOPAQ ®  process (Dutch patent), which involves two steps: sulfate is first anaerobically reduced to sulfide by sulfate-reducing bacteria, and sulfate is then oxidized to elemental sulfur by sulfur-oxidizing bacteria as alkalinity is generated in another reactor. Organic substrates such as hydrogen, ethanol, butanol, or organic waste are used as organic nutrients and electron donors. This method uses less lime and generates a smaller quantity of CMDS compared with conventional methods [ 30 ,  46 ]. As neutralization reactions are not performed, pH remains below 4 during CMDS formation; the resulting CMDS primarily contains goethite. Although over ten systems are operational worldwide, the increasing costs of ethanol and butanol have led to the shutdown of associated projects in South Africa and a gradual decline in the appeal of bioprocesses [ 47 ]. Therefore, CMDS accumulation on membranes is therefore excluded from discussion.

sections.heading: Ion exchange method
paragraphs: Ion exchange uses synthetic resins to swap low-charge ions with high-charge ions from mine wastewater, thereby effectively removing contaminants. This method can selectively target and remove various metals such as copper, nickel, cobalt, zinc, cadmium, lead, mercury, and metalloid arsenic [ 48 ]. The optimal recovery of each element group requires specific ion exchangers or processes [ 47 ]. This approach is highly targeted, but different resins have different influent water quality tolerances, and usually operates most effectively with neutral-to-alkaline mine water [ 49 ]. Therefore, AMD must be pretreated using these methods, and the generation of CMDS from these processes will not be reiterated in subsequent sections.

In active treatment processes, flocculants such as ferric sulfate are added before discharge or sludge removal to enhance the quality of effluents. This improves metal removal via surface adsorption and coprecipitation, as ferric sulfate dissolves rapidly and iron to reprecipitate in the form of ferric hydroxide/hydrated iron. The use of these flocculants typically constitutes 2–5% of treatment costs [ 10 ,  50 ], and their type and concentration considerably influence the properties of existing CMDS.

sections.heading: Passive treatment
paragraphs: Passive treatment requires infrastructure and typically operates without a continuous supply of chemicals or energy, distinguishing it from natural attenuation. This method primarily uses limestone drains, constructed wetlands, reducing and alkalinity-producing systems (RAPSs), successive alkalinity-producing systems (SAPSs), sulfate-reducing bioreactors, vertical flow wetlands, and settling ponds (including settling lagoons), as well as vertical flow reactors [ 51 ,  52 – 53 ].

Anoxic limestone drains (ALD), oxic limestone drains, and open limestone channels are used for limestone draining, all of which operate on the principle of using limestone dissolution to provide alkalinity for AMD and heavy metal precipitation. When the accumulated CMDS clog the system, ALDs cannot longer increase the acid capacity of mine water due to lack of maintenance [ 17 ].

Aerobic and anaerobic wetlands are two types of constructed wetlands. Aerobic wetlands primarily use oxidation and plant action to remove heavy metals, whereas anaerobic wetlands rely on substrates through which AMD flows to form metal sulfides that are immobilized within the wetlands. The density of CMDS in these systems is approximately tenfold that of active mine water treatment [ 54 ]. In general, constructed wetlands serve as a tertiary purification step for AMD pretreated using other methods. For instance, anaerobic wetlands combined with ALDs form RAPSs or SAPSs. Consequently, influent pollutant concentrations in constructed wetlands and CMDS volume are lower, typically accumulating on plant surfaces (leaves and buds); downstream (in rhizomes, roots, and lateral roots); or within the exhausted reactive mix itself [ 52 ]. These precipitates are primarily composed of Fe, Al, Zn, Mn, and PO 4 3− , with the main mineral phases as oxides/hydroxides (predominantly iron oxides); carbonates (such as calcite, siderite, and smithsonite); and sulfides (such as pyrite and gregite) [ 52 ,  55 ,  56 ]. Maintenance, typically dredging, is generally required every 10 to 20 years [ 57 ,  58 ].

In summary, CMDS production in passive treatment is primarily concentrated in the limestone reaction stages, with sludge solids typically exceeding 25% by weight. In the initial stages of the reaction system, CMDS primarily contains iron oxides. Due to the gradual increase in pH, Fe in CMDS often exists as α-FeOOH, which can be processed for eventual reuse [ 27 ,  59 ,  60 ]. Other constituents in CMDS result from the water quality and local environmental conditions, including compounds containing Al and Ca, such as hydroxy-aluminum sulfate ([Al 4 (SO 4 )(OH) 10 ·12–36(H 2 O)]), gypsum, and calcite [ 27 ,  61 ]. Regardless of the treatment method—active or passive—CMDS has a high specific surface area. Its composition is mainly characterized by α-FeOOH, Fe 2 O 3 , CaSO 4 ·xH 2 O, CaO, and CaCO 3 , with proportions varying considerably with treatment methods (Fig.  1 ).

sections.heading: Adsorption of heavy metals (As) from wastewater
paragraphs: CMDS is rich in elements such as Fe, Mn, Si, and Al, and its chemical composition closely resembles that of conventional adsorbents like zeolites—for instance, in terms of Si and Al content. Moreover, it exhibits favorable physicochemical properties, including a high specific surface area (231 m 2  g − 1 ), large pore diameter (52.5 nm), and substantial pore volume (0.41 cm 3  g − 1 ), all of which underscore its potential as an effective adsorbent [ 62 ,  63 ]. Fe in CMDS adsorbs various pollutants, including anions and cations, demonstrating its potential for broad application as an adsorbent. A degree of pretreatment is typically required to enhance the adsorptive properties of these materials [ 64 ]. Table  1  shows the adsorption performance of various materials.

Yang et al. [ 65 ] explored the feasibility of using CMDS to remove arsenite and arsenate from aqueous solutions. At 293 K, the maximum adsorption capacities of CMDS for As(III) and As(V) were 67 and 22 mg g − 1 , respectively, exhibiting superior adsorption performance compared with various natural adsorbents such as iron–manganese sand [ 71 ] and amorphous iron oxides [ 72 ,  73 ]. Ko et al. [ 74 ] used CMDS produced via electrolysis from the Hambeak mine wastewater treatment system in South Korea for arsenate adsorption experiments under laboratory conditions. They achieve maximum adsorption capacities of 59 and 20 mg g − 1  for arsenite and arsenate at pH 7, respectively. Guo et al. [ 66 ] and Kim et al. [ 62 ] synthesized a powdered adsorbent (PCMDS) and a beaded adsorbent (BCMDS) using CMDS treated via electrolysis and precipitation. At 295 K, PCMDS exhibited maximum adsorption capacities of 41 mg g − 1  for As(III) and 65 mg g − 1  for As(V) and BCMDS showed maximum adsorption capacities of 4.6 mg g − 1  for As(III) and 15 mg g − 1  for As(V). PCMDS, with a larger specific surface area, more readily adsorbed As. These adsorbents also possessed a certain capacity for F −  adsorption because new functional groups and pores were formed on the BCMDS surface, which were crucial for arsenic adsorption and one of the key reasons for their superior performance over other natural adsorbents.

Lee et al. [ 69 ] used CMDS from the Taebaek coal mine in South Korea (active method) to synthesize three different adsorbent materials: alginate-modified CMDS beads (AABs), goethite beads modified with alginate (GABs), and pure alginate beads. They revealed that the optimal pH range for As(III) and As(V) adsorption via AABs was 2–10 and 2–9, respectively. On the AAB surface, As(III) and As(V) coexisted; As(III) oxidized to As(V) and enhanced the adsorption capacity of AABs for As(III). Consequently, the maximum adsorption capacity (Q m ) of AABs for As(III) was ~ 18 mg g − 1 , nearly equivalent to its Q m  for As(V) of 22 mg g − 1 . Gupta et al. [ 75 ] revealed that the adsorption of As(III) by manganese-associated hydrous iron(III) oxides was accompanied by its surface oxidation to As(V). The adsorption capacities of AABs for As(III) and As(V) exceeded those of pure alginate beads and alginate-modified GABs, primarily due to the influence of amorphous iron hydroxide on the adsorption levels of As(III) and As(V). Amorphous FeOOH, with its larger surface area, exhibited the highest adsorption capacity [ 76 ]. Extraction experiments were conducted using 0.2 M ammonium oxalate solution, which revealed that the content of amorphous iron hydroxide in CMDS was greater than that of goethite.

Yang et al. [ 65 ] and Guo et al. [ 66 ] posited that As adsorption by CMDS can be elucidated using the pseudo-second-order model and Freundlich isotherm model, indicating that the process is endothermic. The analysis of activation energy suggested that As adsorption involved physisorption and chemisorption, and As reacted with Fe 3+  and Ca 2+  in CMDS to form Ca 3 (AsO 4 ) 2  and FeAsO 4  precipitates. Some arsenates directly adsorbed onto iron oxides more favorably under neutral or slightly acidic conditions. When the pH was lower than the isoelectric point (pH IEP ) of the adsorbent, the surface was positively charged and enhanced As adsorption. Eskandarpour et al. [ 77 ] and Tripathy et al. [ 78 ] also reported similar findings; as the pH increased, deprotonation occurred on the CMDS surface and negative charges (FeO −  groups) became dominant. These changes inhibited As adsorption due to electrostatic repulsion and/or competition with other anions such as hydroxide [ 73 ,  79 ]. Altundoğan et al. [ 80 ] discovered that at pH 7, H 2 AsO 4 −  (40%) and HAsO 4 2−  (60%)— the dominant species of As(V)—were negatively charged; this caused electrostatic repulsion and reduced adsorption capacity. Kim et al. [ 62 ] however found that As(III) adsorption increased with increasing pH between pH IEP (5.3) and 10.2 because within this pH range, the attraction among the negatively charged surface As(III) molecules increased. At weakly basic conditions, no competition was observed between the solid surface H +  ions and As(III) cations. Similar observations were made by Lee et al. [ 69 ] that the optimal pH range for As(III) adsorption was slightly higher than that for As(V) adsorption.

Lee et al. [ 36 ] developed PU-CMDS by incorporating CMDS into granular polyurethane (PU) using a straightforward process(direct immersion approach). Due to the electrostatic nature of PU [ 81 ], the pH IEP  of PU-CMDS increased and enhanced its adsorption capacity for heavy metals. The maximum adsorption capacities for As(III) and As(V) were 16 and 28 mg L − 1 , respectively. Under neutral conditions, PU-CMDS may favor the formation of ≡FeOH 2 + -SO 4 2−  species with negative charges and create repulsion that reduces the adsorption efficiency. Under neutral conditions, sulfates can form outer-sphere complexes with hydrated heavy metals such as Fe [ 82 ], which compete with As(V) [ 83 ]; this mechanism is similar to the inhibition of arsenic adsorption in the presence of phosphates [ 65 ]. Factors such as the number of hydration shells, molecular configuration, and potential magic number effects can further complicate the system [ 84 ]. Figure  2  shows the mechanism of reduced surface adsorption efficiency of As under neutral conditions [ 65 ,  82 ,  83 ,  85 ,  86 – 87 ]. PU-CMDS fabrication process involves sulfate complexation, which diminishes competitive adsorption under neutral conditions and enhances As(V) adsorption capacity. Moreover, Jang [ 88 ] evaluated the adsorption and desorption efficiencies of PU-CMDS using three cycles of medium regeneration and four cycles of column tests, demonstrating its potential for reuse.

Lee et al. [ 67 ,  68 ] investigated the adsorption capacity of CMDS generated via electrolysis before and after the addition of flocculants and found no significant difference in arsenic adsorption between the two types of CMDS. The average correlation coefficients for the Langmuir and Freundlich models were 0.987 and 0.864, respectively, which suggested that increased aggregation did not considerably affect the adsorption capacity. Conversely, Yang et al. [ 70 ] used CMDS from the Jumunjin coal mine in Korea (neutralized with NaOH) to produce iron oxide–coated sand (IOCS), with a mortar-to-CMDS weight ratio of ~ 40:1. The mineralogical composition of the resulting IOCS differed substantially from other CMDS adsorbents that predominantly contained hematite (α-Fe 2 O 3 ), varying proportions of amorphous iron hydroxide/oxide, and a higher sulfate concentration; it also lacked Ca-based reactions. The maximum adsorption capacities were 56 µg g − 1  for As(III) and 99 µg g − 1  for As(V), considerably lower than those of CMDS materials prepared using other methods.

The adsorption of heavy metals by materials fabricated using CMDS was primarily influenced by pH (Fig.  3 ). At pH 3–5, the dominant species of As(III) was uncharged As(OH) 3 ; CMDS carried a positive charge, and Fe existed mainly as ≡FeOH 2 +  and ≡FeOH. The principal complexation form for As(III) was ≡ FeO-As(OH) 3 . For As(V), the dominant species was H 2 AsO 4 −  [ 36 ,  37 ]. Between pH 5 and 6.5, ≡FeOH 2 -H 2 AsO 4  coexisted with ≡ FeO-As(OH) 3  on the adsorbent surface, and at pH 6.5–9.3, ≡FeOH-H 2 AsO 4 , ≡FeOH 2 -H 2 AsO 4 , ≡FeO-H 2 AsO 4 , and ≡ FeO-HAsO 4  were found as surface species [ 62 ]. Above pH 9.5, AsO(OH) 2 −  was the dominant species [ 89 ]. However, As(III) and As(V) absorption by AABs remained unaffected by pH IEP  [ 69 ]. This phenomenon could be attributed to the high affinity of pure alginates derived from brown seaweed for divalent cations [ 90 ,  91 ]. Alginate molecules contained carboxyl groups; thus, the AABs surface carried a negative charge. This specific bonding reaction on the AABs surface prevailed over electrostatic interactions. Jain et al. [ 92 ] reported that adsorption occurred when arsenic ligands were exchanged with functional groups on the surface of iron oxides/hydroxides. Sherman and Randall [ 93 ] found that As(V) adsorption mechanism on goethite, hornblende, hematite, and hydrated iron proceeded via the formation of bidentate binuclear surface complexes. These insights are crucial for understanding and optimizing the adsorption mechanisms of heavy metals, which provide a reliable perspective for the advancement of environmental remediation and water treatment technologies.

To evaluate the application potential of CMDS adsorbents, desorption capacity is a key factor that determines their potential for sustainable use and economic value besides their adsorption performance. Yang et al. [ 65 ] reported that arsenic adsorbed from actual AMD during column adsorption experiments was 43% of the maximum adsorption capacity observed in batch tests. Moreover, subsequent desorption with NaOH released 85% As, indicating its effective desorption performance. Lee et al. [ 36 ] found that As(V) desorption efficiency from PU-CMDS reached 83% and that of other divalent heavy metals such as Zn, Pb, and Cd reached 86–88%, with an average desorption efficiency of 80% over three consecutive desorption cycles. This value was comparable to that of the heavy metal recovery of natural adsorbents such as magnetic adsorbents (80–90%), schwertmannite adsorbents (45–95%), and Fe 3 O 4 /MnO 2  mixed honeycomb coal adsorbents (75–80%) [ 94 ,  95 – 96 ]. Kumar et al. [ 97 ] confirmed the effective adsorption and desorption of As using PU-CMDS, revealing its commercial viability. However, there is still a gap in adsorption efficiency compared to aluminum-based adsorbents developed specifically for adsorption applications (Patent No. 10-1344235). Jang [ 88 ] experimentally demonstrated that the PU-CMDS adsorption column processed over 14,000 bed volumes of arsenic and toxic heavy metals, below the regulatory limits set by the South Korean standards.

In numerous studies that have used CMDS for the adsorption of heavy metals in water bodies exemplified by arsenic, mineral phases were largely characterized via qualitative/semi-quantitative analyses and targeted quantitative analysis was not performed. Consequently, the characteristics of goethite, amorphous iron hydroxides/oxides, and calcite—key components in chemical reactions—were not fully revealed. Thus, the significant differences in the heavy metal adsorption capacities of CMDS were not appropriately elucidated. CMDS adsorbents generally exhibit a higher adsorption efficiency for As(III) at pH ~ 9, whereas the optimal adsorption pH for As(V) tends toward neutrality (pH 7). The proportions of goethite, amorphous iron hydroxides/oxides, and calcite in CMDS at an optimal pH (below the point of zero charge, pH PZC ) are critical for determining its adsorption performance. Moreover, simple CMDS pretreatments such as doping with specific materials can enhance its surface adsorption capacity or decrease pH PZC . This mitigates the impact of system pH on adsorption efficiency and thereby enhances the application prospects of CMDS as an adsorbent. In summary, after simple pretreatment, CMDS retains its capacity for heavy metal adsorption and exhibits potential for effective desorption and reuse. Although the maximum adsorption capacity of pretreated/reprocessed CMDS may decrease compared with that of the original CMDS powder, it may enhance its practical engineering applicability. These investigations provide a scientific foundation for the application of CMDS for water treatment and environmental remediation.

sections.heading: Treatment of organic wastewater as an advanced oxidant
paragraphs: Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) have demonstrated significant efficacy in removing organic compounds and trace contaminants from water bodies [ 98 ,  99 ]. These approaches principally rely on the production of highly reactive hydroxyl radicals (·OH), which are non-selective and highly oxidative, thereby facilitating organic pollutant mineralization. Fenton and Fenton-like reactions, as variants of AOPs, have been widely used for water treatment over the past two decades; therein, Fe 2+  (or Fe 3+ ) ions react with hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) to generate ·OH radicals for purification [ 100 ,  101 ]. However, the cost of chemical reagents is a significant economic challenge in implementing the Fenton process. Therefore, innovative application of CMDS as a waste iron source for Fenton reactions is feasible and represents a sustainable and cost effective alternative strategy.

Tony and Lin [ 102 ] used CMDS obtained via selective precipitation as an iron source to collect AMD downstream of Marion Meadows in the West Run Watershed of Morgantown, West Virginia, USA. Using the Box–Behnken design, the optimal reaction conditions were determined as a pH of 2.7 and CMDS and H 2 O 2  contents of 41 and 398 mg L − 1 , respectively. The best oxidation effect was achieved under these conditions, with COD and TOC removal efficiencies of 73 and 76%, respectively. Under the optimal conditions identified by response surface methodology at pH 2.2, a 20-min oxidation treatment with 40 and 500 mg L − 1  of CMDS and H 2 O 2  could achieve TOC and COD removal efficiencies of 98 and 73%, respectively [ 103 ]. This method was cost effective compared with other treatment processes, although its application was limited by the instability of CMDS properties.

sections.heading: Stabilization of heavy metals in soil
paragraphs: Remediation methods for heavy metal–contaminated soils have been categorized as active and passive. In passive remediation, heavy metal release is stabilized by adding stabilizers that adsorb and precipitate heavy metals [ 104 ,  105 ]. This process reduces the solubility or mobility of pollutants in soil, ultimately reducing the risk and toxicity caused to humans and ecosystems [ 36 ,  37 ,  106 ]. Typically, valuable waste resources are selected as soil stabilizers to control costs. The potential and limitations of CMDS as a soil stabilizer are subsequently discussed.

sections.heading: Utilization of CMDS for stabilizing contaminated soil
paragraphs: Cui et al. [ 107 ] introduced CMDS (produced via electrolysis) into heavy metal–contaminated soil and conducted column leaching tests based on variations in precipitation and pH. Results revealed that soil containing 3 wt% CMDS exhibited the lowest heavy metal leaching concentrations during an acidic rainfall (pH < 3.3). Ko et al. [ 74 ] incorporated 3 wt% CMDS generated via electrolysis into As-contaminated soil, which considerably reduced arsenic release by 24 µg L − 1 . These findings collectively suggest that CMDS can effectively diminish the release of heavy metals from soil, positioning it as a potential material for stabilizing heavy metals in contaminated soils.

sections.heading: Synergistic stabilization of contaminated soil using different wastes and CMDS
paragraphs: Heavy metals in rare earth–contaminated sites have been immobilized using mixtures of various wastes. Moon et al. [ 108 ] treated soil with 10 wt% CMDS, which reduced the As leaching efficiency by ~ 72%. When the soil was stabilized using a combination of 10 wt% CMDS and calcined oyster shells (COS), the leaching efficiencies of the three target contaminants (As, Cu, and Pb) were considerably reduced after a 28-d stabilization period. More than 93% of As was reduced, and over 99% of copper and lead reductions were observed. X-ray absorption near edge structure results indicated that arsenic predominantly existed in its pentavalent form, with no significant change compared to the control group. Scanning electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy revealed that arsenic immobilization could be associated with the formation of calcium arsenate [ 109 ,  110 ] and iron arsenate precipitates [ 108 ,  111 ,  112 ]. The immobilization of lead and copper was likely related to calcium silicate hydrates (CSHs) and calcium aluminate hydrates (CAHs) [ 113 ,  114 ]. In the liquid phase, the compounds that absorbed and precipitated heavy metals were primarily composed of Fe and Ca. This technology is currently being used to treat heavy metal–contaminated soils at a military firing range and at sites wherein wood is treated with chromated copper arsenate [ 108 ].

Lee et al. [ 115 ] developed a stabilizer composed of COS and CMDS. Under 0.1 M HCl extraction conditions, this stabilizer considerably reduced the leaching of arsenic, lead, and copper from soil and their reduction efficiencies exceeded 90% compared with that observed in control experiments. Kang et al. [ 116 ] conducted field trials and found that CMDS outperformed other waste materials such as limestone and steelmaking slag (SMS) in reducing arsenic content in soil and rice; this process decreased the concentration of extractable arsenic in the soil solution by 60–92%. Cui et al. [ 117 ] compared the effectiveness of waste materials such as SMS and waste cow bone (WCB), revealing that the material prepared in the laboratory using a 1:1 ratio of CMDS and SMS (SM) was the most stable. When incorporated into contaminated soil at an optimal ratio of 7 wt%, the arsenic concentration in the extract decreased from an initial concentration of 3.5 to ~ 0.001 mg L − 1  after a 4-d stabilization period. In a field experiment conducted in an agricultural area in Yixing, China, the initial arsenic concentration in the extract decreased from 3.5 mg L − 1  to undetectable levels after a 10-d stabilization period. During the experiment, the pH increased above 9 and the effects remained stable after 150 days. These studies clearly demonstrate the enhanced stabilization effects of CMDS on heavy metals in contaminated soils when it was applied along with other types of calcium-based waste materials.

Arsenic stabilization can be achieved via complexation with α-FeOOH using complexes such as ≡FeOAsO 2 , ≡FeOAsOOH, ≡FeOAs(OH) 2 , and ≡FeOAsOH [ 93 ], precipitation reactions, potentially through the leaching of Fe from FeOOH to form FeAsO 4  [ 118 ], and the formation of Ca 3 (AsO4) 2  [ 110 ]. Arsenic stability can be enhanced with increased CMDS application, elevated soil pH levels, and extended stabilization periods. The stability of arsenic is maintained even under simulated acid rain conditions (pH below 3.3), possibly due to the formation of stable arsenic complexes induced by the addition of a stabilizer [ 115 ]. The primary component of CMDS, α-FeOOH, effectively stabilizes arsenic [ 119 ], whereas its calcareous components, such as CSH and CAH, form complexes with heavy metals, thereby further enhancing arsenic stabilization [ 120 ,  121 ].

sections.heading: Utilizing CMDS to mitigate impacts on soil health
paragraphs: The stabilizing effect of various waste materials on heavy metal–contaminated soils has been extensively studied; however, the restoration of soil fertility and physicochemical properties are scarcely studied. Thus, the suitability of soils for agricultural use has not been sufficiently evaluated. Kim et al. [ 122 ] recently explored the overall suitability of soils stabilized with AMD sludge (AMDS), CMDS, steel slag, lime, and cement. They introduced soil health index (SHI) to comprehensively assess factors such as soil productivity, stability, and biodiversity. Results showed the total SHI of differently treated soils as follows: control soil (1.90) > heavy metal–contaminated soil (1.55) > CMDS-stabilized soil (1.29) > steel slag-stabilized soil (1.29) > AMDS-stabilized soil (1.26) > cement-stabilized soil (0.74) > lime-stabilized soil (0.67). Before using a stabilizer, the SHI of heavy metal–contaminated soil was within the “normal” range. However, most soils treated with stabilizers showed a deterioration in general, primarily manifested as increased electrical conductivity and decreased available phosphorus. Upon adding CMDS into the soil and subjecting the soil to long-term acid rain leaching, heavy metals in the soil could potentially be activated. McDonald et al. [ 123 ] and Chi et al. [ 124 ] revealed that the soil pH decreased by 0.09 to 0.25 units after 12 months, thereby increasing the extractable As, Cd, Cu, and Zn contents by an average of 34, 16, 21, and 15%, respectively. This result differed from those of Lee et al. [ 115 ], it may be related to localized factors such as the time span of the study, the experimental scale, and the heavy metal content in the CMDS [ 125 ]. In conclusion, although the addition of stabilizers reduced the leaching rate of heavy metals, it negatively affected the physicochemical properties of soil. Ions precipitated from stabilizers also possibly further decreased the soil health. Therefore, soils treated with stabilizers may not yet be suitable for agricultural use or the relevant technologies for determining their suitability may not be mature.

sections.heading: Recommendations for using CMDS as a sediment stabilizer
paragraphs: When the focus shifts from soil remediation—particularly of agricultural land—to the solidification of contaminated lake sediments or other types of sludge, the impact on soil physicochemical properties is no longer a primary concern. Kim et al. [ 126 ] demonstrated the potential of this application by investigating the stabilization effect of CMDS on heavy metals in rare earth wastewater sludge. Their study revealed that mixing 10% CMDS with the sediment effectively removed As and Se, achieving removal efficiencies of 76 and 67%, respectively. In another study, Moon et al. [ 108 ] examined the stabilization of As- and Pb-contaminated sediments from Lake Nakdong and the Yeongsan River in South Korea using combinations of COS, WCB, and CMDS. The results showed that a mixture of 10 wt% COS and 5 wt% CMDS yielded the best performance in arsenic immobilization. After treatment, the HCl-extractable As concentration in the sediment dropped to 7.9 mg kg − 1 , representing a reduction of 63%. Notably, iron-arsenic precipitates were found to be more effective than calcium-arsenic precipitates in reducing arsenic leachability, suggesting that CMDS offers superior stabilization performance compared to COS alone.

The heavy metal stabilization mechanism of CMDS primarily relies on its abundant iron and aluminum oxide components, which provide high specific surface area and active adsorption sites. These constituents enable the stable binding of heavy metals through various mechanisms such as surface complexation, ion exchange, and co-precipitation. For example, As(V) can form monodentate or bidentate inner-sphere complexes with iron (hydr)oxides under neutral to slightly alkaline conditions [ 127 ]. In addition, Ca 2+ , Fe 3+ , and Al 3+  ions present in CMDS can act as cationic bridging agents, promoting the precipitation of arsenate as insoluble calcium arsenates or facilitating its encapsulation under high pH conditions [ 128 ].

For heavy metals such as Pb, Zn, and Cd, stabilization can occur via precipitation as hydroxides or carbonates in the environment modified by CMDS. Studies have shown that Pb can be immobilized with efficiencies exceeding 90%, while Zn stabilization efficiencies are typically above 80% [ 129 ]. Furthermore, the pH elevation induced by CMDS contributes to reduced metal mobility in soils and sediments, which is particularly critical for specific adsorption mechanisms involving iron oxides. For instance, hydroxyl groups on the surface of minerals like Fe(OH) 3  can coordinate with metal ions to form inner-sphere complexes, thereby enhancing their stability [ 130 ]. Arsenic immobilization is largely dependent on the ability of Fe/Al oxides to form mono- or bidentate complexes with arsenate, with calcium further strengthening precipitation and bridging interactions [ 128 ].

However, potential environmental side effects of CMDS must also be considered. The iron-bearing mineral phases in CMDS may alter redox conditions in sediments due to their oxidative or catalytic properties, potentially impacting microbial communities and influencing the release of nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus—thereby exacerbating the risk of eutrophication [ 20 ,  131 ]. Additionally, current research has not yet comprehensively assessed the release of pollutants such as SO 4 2− , Fe 2+ /Fe 3+  from the overlying water of CMDS-treated sediments, highlighting the need for enhanced monitoring of such risks in future studies.

The distribution patterns of heavy metals in soils and sediments are influenced not only by CMDS treatment but also by factors such as pH, organic matter content, redox conditions, and ionic competition. Low pH values can protonate adsorption sites, weaken metal binding, and dissolve iron and manganese oxides, leading to the release of adsorbed heavy metals [ 130 ,  132 ]. Organic matter, rich in carboxyl and phenolic hydroxyl groups, can enhance stabilization through complexation with metal ions, although soluble organic acids may also promote metal mobility [ 130 ]. Under reducing conditions, Fe(III) oxides may dissolve and As(V) may be reduced to the more mobile As(III), often resulting in arsenic release [ 131 ]. Moreover, cations such as Ca 2+  and Na +  may suppress heavy metal immobilization by competing for adsorption sites, while anions like PO 4 3−  can compete with arsenate for binding, thereby enhancing arsenic mobility [ 133 ,  134 ].

In summary, the application of CMDS-derived stabilizing agents for the remediation of heavy metal-contaminated soils may lead to significant changes in soil physicochemical properties, potentially affecting key indicators such as biodiversity and soil productivity. In practical scenarios such as agricultural cultivation and irrigation, reducing conditions in the rhizosphere may alter the chemical speciation of metals—for example, promoting the transformation of As(V) to the more toxic As(III). While stabilization treatments can effectively immobilize heavy metals, their potential side effects should not be overlooked. Therefore, before repurposing such stabilized soils for agricultural production, it is advisable to adopt precautionary measures—such as covering with clean topsoil or implementing a period of environmental monitoring—to ensure their safe and sustainable use.

sections.heading: As a barrier layer
paragraphs: The potential application of CMDS as a liner and cover material for landfill sites has garnered research interest. Lee et al. [ 68 ] prepared a CMDS liner by mixing CMDS with bentonite and cement in a 1:0.5:0.3 ratio; they achieved an initial permeability of 7.1 × 10 − 7  cm s − 1 , and the leachate tests met environmental standards. Lee et al. [ 67 ] subsequently simulated the performance of this liner after seven freeze–thaw cycles at -20 °C, which revealed that the bentonite–cement mixture maintained a compressive strength above 5 kg cm − 2 , meeting US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) requirements [ 135 ]. However, post freeze–thaw permeability increased to 9.8 × 10 − 7  cm s − 1 , approximately 1.5 times the initial rate. Despite an increase in permeability under the freeze–thaw and wet–dry cycles and minor variations in water content, the mixture was considered suitable as a barrier material for landfill final covers and drainage layers based on the US EPA standards. However, the reported permeability did not meet the Chinese requirements for critical antiseepage areas such as landfills, where the permeability coefficient should be ≤ 10 − 7  cm s − 1  [ 136 ]. Moreover, evaluating mechanical performance solely based on compressive strength is inadequate because local fractures can cause leachate infiltration and groundwater contamination, posing severe consequences for any region. Therefore, the use of CMDS for landfill liner applications requires further research to ensure its environmental safety and reliability in practical applications.

As a cover for tailings storage facilities or landfill caps, where stringent mechanical properties and permeability requirements are less critical, CMDS can effectively block precipitation and oxygen. Sephton et al. [ 137 ] mixed 15% CMDS with Portland cement and fly ash to form a liner material, which was then applied to sulfur-containing waste rock in Brukunga, South Australia. In ~ one year, this composite liner considerably reduced the generation of AMD and reduced the acidity, metal content, and sulfate loads in the leachate by 80–95%; this value was comparable to that obtained without the addition of cement. AMDS did not release its adsorbed heavy metals, and the mixture demonstrated a favorable cost-to-benefit ratio. A recent study by Ma et al. [ 138 ] revealed that gel composites prepared from CMDS formed an organic–inorganic hybrid network structure, achieving a water retention efficiency of 58.6% at 100 °C. This effectively prevents moisture loss and coal oxidation, making the material suitable for application in coal stockpiles to suppress spontaneous combustion.

Chi et al. [ 124 ] examined the capability of CMDS (treated via lime neutralization) to support plant growth, mitigate acidification, and immobilize heavy metals in mine waste rock recovery. They found that Bermuda grass exhibited good adaptability to nutrient deficiency and heavy metal stress [ 139 ], with a significant increase in biomass due to enhanced soil nutrients and enzymatic activity when chemical fertilizers and chicken manure compost were used. Without fertilization, all plants, including  Medicago sativa  L. and  Paspalum wettsteinii  Hack, survived in CMDS. Over time, vegetation cover and soil development can reduce soil salinity [ 140 ]. However, nutrient deficiencies and the potential re-release of heavy metals remain major limiting factors for the application of CMDS as a growth substrate [ 106 ,  141 ,  142 – 143 ]. Notably, when CMDS is applied at higher rates to increase nutrient inputs, the leaching behavior of the added fertilizers becomes critical, as it can alter the mineralization of organic nitrogen and phosphorus. Moreover, Chi et al. [ 124 ] highlighted the need to maintain certain levels of ammonia and bioavailable phosphorus in modified CMDS to benefit plant growth. The necessity of continuous fertilization, impact of plant litter on land reclamation, and long-term field-scale assessment of microbial biomass and diversity must be particularly studied in the future.

sections.heading: Treatment of rare earth element wastewater
paragraphs: Various pollutants are released via leaching during rare earth element mining, including ammonium ions (NH 4 + ), sulfate ions (SO 4 2− ), phosphate ions (PO 4 3− ), fluoride ions (F − ), multiple heavy metals (Zn, Cd, Pb, Cu, and As), radioactive substances (thorium (Th), uranium (U)), and organic solvents (bis(2-ethylhexyl) phosphate (P 5 O 7 , C 16 H 35 O 3 P), and oxalic acid (H 2 C 2 O 4 )) [ 135 ]. These contaminants pose a significant environmental threat, thereby necessitating that rare earth mining companies implement effective pollution control and remediation measures to mitigate their environmental impact.

Cui et al. [ 144 ] developed a novel and economical sequential process that comprised precipitation, adsorption, and oxidation for rare earth element wastewater treatment. The process employed pretreated PU-CMDS to remove residual anions and radioactive contaminants such as U and Th after precipitation. At pH 6.5, Th/U removal was facilitated by ≡FeOH 2 +  −SO 4 2−  complexation. Below pH 5, Th/U initially reacted with HCO 3 −  to form complexes and then with ≡FeOH 2 + −SO 4 2− . At pH < 3.5, Th/U concentrations were relatively low. The system achieved removal efficiencies of 99.9–100% for heavy metals, 99.3–99.9% for F and As, 95.8–99.4% for U and Th, and 92.4% for COD Cr . Lee et al. [ 145 ] refined this process further and used PU-CMDS for the adsorption stage and a pilot study. They achieved removal efficiencies for As, F, Th, Pb, and COD Cr  in rare earth element wastewater of 99.8, ~ 100, 93.6, ~ 100, and 88.8%, respectively; the effluent quality met EPA and China’s recommended limits for irrigation pollutants. Although CMDS shows potential as a material for treating rare earth element wastewater, the associated transportation costs cannot be overlooked.

sections.heading: Phosphate adsorption
paragraphs: Low-crystalline iron oxyhydroxides such as α-FeOOH and lepidocrocite (β-FeOOH) have garnered attention for their exceptional adsorptive properties when used for studying phosphate adsorption characteristics. These materials retain their adsorption efficacy even after undergoing 10 adsorption/desorption cycles [ 146 ]. Based on this finding, the phosphate adsorption capabilities of CMDS containing similar components have been extensively studied.

Sapsford et al. [ 147 ] performed acid leaching on CMDS produced from six active and passive mine water treatment sites in the United Kingdom to extract derivative reagents. Results revealed that at pH 6–8.6, the derived reagents achieved phosphate removal efficiencies of > 97%. These findings were not considerably different from those of laboratory-prepared ferric chloride solutions used as a control. Sibrell et al. [ 148 ] used CMDS from the Brandy Camp Blue Valley mine in Pennsylvania, USA, and created a fixed bed after drying and screening for a pilot test. The system operated continuously for 46 days and achieved a phosphate removal efficiency of up to 96%.

Abed et al. [ 149 ] mixed Portland cement with CMDS in the Deerplay coal mine wastewater treatment plant in Rochdale, Lancashire, UK a 3:7 ratio via neutralization to obtain CMDS adsorption particles. These particles were then used to treat synthetic high- and low-concentration greywater. Results revealed phosphate adsorption efficiencies of 71 and 56% in high- and low-concentration greywater, respectively. Compared with the control group wherein only cement was used as an adsorbent, the CMDS adsorbent reduced the retention time of the system. This effect was attributed to the strong adsorption capacity of phosphates by the oxides or hydroxides of iron and aluminum and the calcium compounds released by the CMDS adsorbent [ 150 ]. However, some side effects are involved when using CMDS as an adsorbent such as a significant increase in turbidity, total suspended solids, and effluent color; these can adversely impact the water quality. When using CMDS adsorbents in practical wastewater treatment processes, these parameters must be strictly controlled and managed.

Ahmed et al. [ 151 ] experimentally studied iron-based sludge collected from a Fe(III)-dosed anaerobic bioreactor. The sludge primarily contained components such as α-Fe 2 O 3  (hematite), γ-Fe 2 O 3  (maghemite), and Fe 3 O 4  (magnetite) and was highly similar CMDS. After calcination at different temperatures (350 and 500 °C), magnetized iron oxide particles were produced. Their magnetic properties were influenced by the crystallinity of the sludge material. The samples calcined at 350 °C exhibited superior phosphate adsorption performance owing to their higher specific surface area and improved magnetic properties, with the adsorption capacity reaching 31–35 mg g − 1  [ 149 ].

Dobbie et al. [ 152 ] further investigated the phosphorus removal efficiency of CMDS (predominantly composed of hematite) at the Leitholm wastewater treatment plant in Scotland. Over a nine-month pilot study, an 80% removal efficiency of the influent total phosphorus was achieved, with an average daily removal of 65 ± 48 mg of total phosphorus (mg TP kg − 1  d − 1 ). The system was designed to allow influent to flow upward from the bottom, which passed through the CMDS material layer before overflowing into the wetland. Results revealed that over time, the growth of biofilms and accumulation of organic matter clogged the interstitial spaces between fill materials; this caused poor aeration and reductive conditions. This issue can be prevented via pretreatment to remove organic matter and suspended solids before the influent entered the system. However, due to the inherent alkalinity of CMDS, already adsorbed phosphorus is not released again [ 153 ,  154 ]. Similar pilot studies at the Windlestone wastewater treatment plant in England after three years of operation showed that CMDS did not release harmful substances, demonstrating its good operational efficiency [ 152 ]. Wei et al. [ 155 ] treated secondary effluent from an actual urban wastewater treatment plant using CMDS that was actively treated with ammonia in North Central West Virginia, USA, and achieved up to 98% of phosphorus removal efficiency. Beyond applications in wastewater treatment plants, the potential of CMDS in removing phosphorus from agricultural runoff has also been confirmed [ 156 ,  157 ,  158 – 159 ]. Moreover, CMDS has been successfully used in the treatment of high-phosphorus emulsion wastewater [ 14 ].

The adsorption efficiency of phosphates is closely linked to the pH of water, which can be explained by the PZC of minerals such as magnetite and hematite. The PZC refers to the pH at which the surface of a solid has an equal amount of positive and negative charges; these charges affect the adsorptive capacity of solids for ions [ 160 ,  161 ]. Below the PZC, the surface of magnetite and hematite was positively charged and favored the adsorption of negatively charged phosphate ions. In contrast, above PZC, the surface becomes negatively charged and its capacity to adsorb negatively charged phosphate ions is reduced. Under alkaline conditions, phosphate removal mechanisms may shift from adsorption to precipitation with calcium ions and form insoluble calcium phosphate. Heal et al. [ 156 ] and Dobbie et al. [ 152 ] suggested that phosphate removal in alkaline conditions may involve chemical precipitation as well as adsorption. As CMDS is alkaline, it may facilitate the precipitation of phosphates with calcium at higher pH. The adsorption efficiency of magnetized iron oxides (such as calcined products of magnetite and hematite) for phosphorus may also be maximized at a relatively low pH range. This indicates that in practical applications, the pH of water must be controlled to ensure the highest phosphorus removal efficiency. This highlights the importance of pH control and adjustment during the design of phosphorus removal systems.

The longevity of CMDS as a phosphorus adsorbent is primarily attributed to its resistance to saturation after phosphate adsorption, which allows CMDS-derived phosphorus adsorbents to maintain their adsorption activity over extended periods even under high-phosphorus loads. Consequently, the frequency of replacement and associated treatment costs are reduced. After CMDS adsorbents reach adsorption saturation, they can be repurposed as slow-release fertilizers [ 162 ]. This approach not only addresses the phosphorus content in wastewater but also recovers and transforms it into a resource for agricultural production. Moreover, slow-release fertilizers gradually provide phosphorus for plant uptake, thereby enhancing fertilizer efficiency and reducing environmental pollution. Dobbie et al. [ 163 ] and Cucarella et al. [ 164 ] reported that using saturated CMDS adsorbents as slow-release fertilizers does not adversely affect crop yield, plant, or soil quality.

These demonstrated that CMDS effectively removed phosphorus from water bodies and enabled agricultural repurposing, thereby addressing soil contamination by heavy metals while providing essential nutrients. This recycling strategy exemplified sustainable development by minimizing waste generation and transforming waste into valuable resources.

sections.heading: Wastewater decolorization
paragraphs: Under anaerobic conditions in the environment, azo dyes in textile wastewater may decompose into aromatic amines with potential carcinogenic risks [ 165 ,  166 ]. The widely used treatment technologies, such as activated carbon adsorption, oxidative treatment, and chemical coagulation, are cost-prohibitive [ 167 ,  168 – 169 ]. In contrast, positively charged waste iron hydroxides and oxides are seen as promising alternatives for efficiently removing anionic dyes [ 170 ].

Netpradit et al. [ 171 ] investigated the removal efficiency and mechanism of metal hydroxides for azo reactive dyes; these are chemically similar to CMDS and primarily composed of calcium and iron obtained via treatment with lime and ferrous sulfate. At the optimal adsorption pH of 8–9—near the zero charge point of sludge—these materials exhibited high adsorption capacity for azo reactive dyes; the maximum adsorption capacity ranged from 48 to 62 mg g − 1  dye adsorbent. The highest decolorization efficiencies for RR-141, RR-120, and RR-2 dyes were 98, 90, and 50%, respectively. The adsorption process followed the Freundlich isotherm model, and the adsorbed reactive dyes were effectively desorbed by alkali washing (0.01 M NaOH) with a desorption efficiency of ~ 100%. This process is considered an ionic exchange between the anionic groups (-SO 3 − ) in dyes and hydroxyl groups (OH − ) in the sludge [ 172 ,  173 ]. This makes the anionic content (-SO 3 − ) of the dyes a key factor that affects the adsorption performance of the metal hydroxide sludge. Wei and Viadero [ 174 ] used CMDS from a mine in North Central West Virginia that was processed with hydrogen peroxide and anhydrous ammonia to adsorb the azo dye Congo Red via a precoating technique. They found a maximum adsorption capacity of 389 mg g − 1  and a dye removal efficiency of up to 95%. Results indicated that adsorption primarily occurred on the surface of CMDS sludge particles, with an optimal pH between 8 and 9. The adsorption capacity decreased when the pH exceeded 8.5. The adsorption process conformed to the pseudo-second-order kinetic model and was exothermic.

In summary, the potential of CMDS in removing azo reactive dyes and its practicality for decolorizing during textile wastewater treatment processes highlighted its significant advantages. Although the CMDS-treated wastewater may release some metals, these can be effectively removed in subsequent precipitation steps. The lower cost of CMDS compared with that of traditional materials such as activated carbon further enhanced its viability as a wastewater treatment medium.

sections.heading: Preparation of inorganic pigments
paragraphs: The extraction and precipitation of CMDS from AMD to produce inorganic pigments suitable for the ceramic industry represent an effective method for the resource utilization of heavy metals. Lopez-Navarrete et al. [ 175 ] reported that inorganic pigments must remain insoluble within the glaze matrix and exhibit appropriate physical properties that matched those of the final product such as excellent wear resistance and environmental resilience. Inorganic pigments primarily contain a host phase embedded with chromophore elements, which are typically transition metal cations that cause coloration. Muñoz et al. [ 176 ] suggested that the crystal structure into which the chromophore elements were embedded may be relatively simple, including transition metal oxides such as Fe 2 O 3 , which can form colored crystals with limited solubility in glass matrices [ 177 ]. These crystals undergo calcination and can thermodynamically stabilize and form colored spinels. Consequently, they meet the requirements of the ceramic industry for inorganic pigments [ 178 ].

As CMDS is rich in iron oxides, its potential in the production of ceramic pigments has been widely explored [ 58 ,  179 ]. Kirby et al. [ 58 ] comparatively analyzed 43 untreated and treated (both actively and passively using wetlands) CMDS samples using five yellow-red pigments. They characterized the iron content and iron mineral phases in detail, positing the hypothesis that CMDS may be an underexploited pigment resource. They underscored the value of CMDS as a potential pigment resource and laid the groundwork for further research and application.

Marcello et al. [ 180 ] found that calcined CMDS can only be used as a pigment when mixed with pure oxides or as a component of commercial pigments. When used alone, calcined CMDS residues appear faded brown and are therefore unsuitable as pigments for ceramic glazes. CMD exhibits relatively better results when mixed with other substances, although it still falls short compared to commercial pigments. Seo et al. [ 181 ] and de Almeida Silva et al. [ 182 ,  183 ] suggested that this phenomenon was possibly caused by strong alkalis in the raw CMDS, which precipitate over a broad pH range and yield a mixture containing heavy metal oxides such as Fe, Mn, and Al and a high Fe 2+ /Fe 3+  ratio. These contents affect the final coloration outcome of calcined CMDS.

Hedin [ 61 ] revealed that CMDS obtained via active treatment methods was impure, whereas those derived from passive treatment systems were purer and highly suitable for pigment applications. This was attributed to the addition of strong or weak alkalis in active treatments that rapidly increased pH, thereby precipitating over 90% of heavy metals in AMD. In contrast, passive systems allow for a slower pH increase and typically yield higher purity metal oxide precipitates [ 181 ,  182 ,  184 ,  185 ]. Hedin [ 61 ] further suggested that the optimal conditions for repurposing CMDS as a pigment via reuse were a pH of 6–7, specifically within passive treatment processes.

sections.heading: Recycling for AMD wastewater treatment
paragraphs: The ability of CMDS generated from wastewater treatment systems to adsorb heavy metals from wastewater was previously studied. Thus, CMDS can be effectively used in the in situ or ex situ treatment of AMD, where it demonstrated excellent adsorption efficiency. It achieved the coprecipitation of heavy metals while utilizing its alkaline properties to neutralize the pH of wastewater and reducing the reagent costs. After ~ 70 days of continuous pilot-scale treatment of actual acidic mine water from a lead–zinc mine, the high and low loadings of CMDS effectively removed various heavy metals. At a high CMDS loading (560 g L − 1 ), Zn(II) concentration decreased from approximately 44 mg L − 1  to below 1 mg L − 1  and showed good removal efficiency for other heavy metals such as Fe and Cu. However, Mn removal was not significant, possibly because Mn was precipitated at a higher pH range. High CMDS loading, although effective, may cause mechanical damage and pooling problems in the mixed system. Therefore, an optimal CMDS loading of 280 g L − 1  is recommended [ 186 ].

sections.heading: Methods to optimize CMDS properties: selective precipitation for the directed preparation of CMDS
paragraphs: Existing AMD treatment techniques primarily focus on adjusting the pH of AMD and removing heavy metals such as Fe and Mn, which yield CMDS mixed with various substances. In contrast, selective precipitation processes aim at resource recovery and specifically target the recovery of dissolved metals such as Fe, Al, and Mn in AMD. This yielded comparatively pure CMDS and simplified subsequent processing (Table  2 ). Selective precipitation methods typically include microbiological, chemical, and electrolytic processes; however, the coprecipitation of metals such as Fe and Al at low pH remains a challenge [ 188 ,  189 ]. This limits the efficiency and purity of metal recovery from AMD.

Wei et al. [ 184 ] developed a two-step selective precipitation process to recover high-purity iron and aluminum from AMD. During this process, iron precipitates as hydroxides at a pH of 3.5–4.0 and achieve a purity of 93.4% and a recovery efficiency of 99%. After iron removal, the resulting AMD water was used to recover aluminum at a pH of 6.0–7.0. Herein, the aluminum precipitation was optimal, with a recovery efficiency of 97% and a purity of 92%. This extraction method, without oxidation pretreatment, may yield CMDS with higher impurity content, particularly with considerable amounts of ferrous hydroxide in the aluminum precipitates. Seo et al. [ 181 ] used wastewater from the Samma-Taejeong coal mine in Korea and used a three-step selective precipitation method for heavy metal recovery. They used NaOH, Ca(OH) 2 , and Na 2 CO 3  based on the selective precipitation characteristics of heavy metals at different pH. Fe(OH) 3  yields a lower-solubility product compared with Fe(OH) 2 , meaning that Fe 3+  has considerably lower solubility than Fe 2+  at the same pH [ 190 ]. Thus, by preoxidizing Fe 2+  with hydrogen peroxide, the iron recovery efficiency considerably increased from 45 to 70 to 99–99% at pH 4.5. At pH 5.5, the aluminum recovery efficiency reached 70–82% with a purity of 94–99.9%. Post-oxidation at pH 8.5 increased the recovery efficiency to 37–87%. Bok et al. [ 187 ] studied AMD obtained from the Samma-Taejeong coal mine in Korea and found that iron was completely precipitated at pH 4, whereas aluminum completely precipitated after pH 5. The iron recovery efficiencies reached 99.8% and a purity of 96%, and aluminum recovery efficiencies of 90% were achieved with a purity of 75%. This suggested that the AMD underwent sufficient aeration before entering the system and iron was completely precipitated at lower pH. Chen et al. [ 185 ] conducted selective precipitation on wastewater from the Dabaoshan mine area in Guangdong Province at different pH ranges and successfully recovered CMDS containing Fe, Cu, Zn, and Mn, with respective recovery efficiencies of 99, 86, 87, and 79%. They also explored the potential applications of these recovered materials during the preparation of iron oxide red, flotation of Cu and Zn, and the production of Mn-containing cement mixtures. The recovered Fe precipitates were amorphous, whereas the Al precipitates were CaSO 4 ·0.5H 2 O. These studies focused primarily on the recovery of metallic substances, without detailed differentiation of the forms and mineral compositions of metals.

In addition to pH, the choice of neutralizing agent is critical for the extraction of heavy metal mineral phases. de Almeida Silva et al. [ 182 ] used NaOH as a neutralizing agent to treat AMD from a coal slag deposit in Santa Catarina, Brazil, at pH 3.5 ~ 3.7 and successfully extracted high-purity iron CMDS. This CMDS was used to produce high-purity goethite pigments; they found that incorporating it into cement at a 1:10 ratio effectively colored the cement paste. de Almeida Silva et al. [ 183 ] subsequently added a weaker base, i.e., NaHCO 3 , at pH 3.5 ~ 3.7 [ 188 ] for precipitating trivalent iron from AMD. By aerating with compressed air for 24 h, they oxidized divalent Fe 2+  to trivalent Fe 3+  and caused iron hydroxide precipitation. Using potassium hydroxide, they obtained well-formed α-FeOOH that had similar morphology to commercial goethite and with more perfected shapes than the goethite samples obtained from AMD [ 182 ]. Using weak bases as neutralizing agents may yield higher extraction efficiency for the selective precipitation of CMDS to produce goethite. Seo et al. [ 181 ] successfully obtained pigmentary goethite and hematite via selective iron precipitation; these sludges were then used to create colored mortars [ 182 ]. When selectively producing goethite, Al interference must be minimized by controlling conditions because aluminum content adversely affected the formation of goethite crystals [ 191 ,  192 ].

The tendency of Fe and Al to co-precipitate at pH of 4.5–5.5 is one of the factors that affect the purity of selectively precipitated CMDS. Menezes et al. [ 193 ] however exploited this characteristic and precipitated Fe and Al at pH 5. They then dissolved them in sulfuric acid to produce a coagulant composed of 8.7% iron and 3.3% aluminum. Wastewater treatment tests demonstrated that this coagulant performed comparably to conventional coagulants used in water treatment plants. This process could be easily integrated into traditional AMD treatment facilities, which mitigated the generation of sludge waste and transformed the waste into a commercially valuable chemical reagent.

Biomining can also be used to selectively precipitate specific minerals, particularly schwertmannite (Fe 8 O 8 (OH) 6 (SO 4 )·nH 2 O) that was first described in 1990 [ 194 ]. It can efficiently extract this mineral from AMD, typically involving a system of aeration tanks and oxidation chambers. The oxidation chamber contains biofilm carriers, and at pH 2.5–3.3, Schwertmannite is precipitated on the biofilm carriers and suspended microbes in the chamber. A chain scraper at the bottom of the oxidation chamber continuously removed CMDS to a sludge collection pool. The collected Schwertmannite has significant potential applications in wastewater treatment, catalyst preparation, and materials science [ 195 ,  196 – 197 ].

Selective precipitation is an effective means to recover heavy metal resources from AMD, which offers enhanced economic benefits via the recovery of high-value by-products and addresses operational disruptions or abandonment issues due to insufficient post-operational funding in unowned AMD treatment facilities. Current efforts in metal recovery focus on two target orientations: the recovery of specific metal elements and acquisition of specific metal mineral phases. These orientations provide critical parameters such as pH and precipitant type required for selective precipitation. The valence state of Fe ions and pH range must be strictly controlled (Table  3 ; Fig.  4 ) [ 181 ,  183 ,  190 ,  191 ,  193 ]. However, the variability of factors such as surface precipitation, groundwater seepage, and mineral dissolution cause fluctuations in influent characteristics. This poses challenges for comprehensive automation control technologies. In practice, detailed selection and adjustment should be made based on local conditions. Moreover, selective precipitation may yield better results for mine wastewater with relatively stable effluent quality and volume, thereby improving the environmental benefits of AMD treatment and providing a viable economic solution for mine area environmental management.

sections.heading: Limitations in the application of CMDS
paragraphs: In various resource utilization scenarios, CMDS faces corresponding constraints. Overall, the key limiting factors for the future valorization of CMDS are two-fold: the economic value and extractability of beneficial elements, and the potential for secondary release of hazardous components.

sections.heading: Purity and extractability of valuable elements
paragraphs: CMDS is enriched with valuable elements such as Fe, Al, and Mn, offering promising prospects for material applications and metal recovery. However, its practical utilization is hindered by the complex chemical forms of these metals and the difficulty of extraction. As discussed previously, iron in CMDS predominantly exists as α-FeOOH, Fe 2 O 3 , and Fe(OH) 3 , accounting for over 90% of the iron content, especially in CMDS derived from electrocoagulation or neutralization processes [ 37 ,  38 ]. Although these oxides are iron-rich, their structural stability makes them resistant to dissolution under neutral conditions, often requiring intensified methods such as acid leaching.

Additionally, calcium and aluminum typically exist in CMDS as CaSO 4 , CaCO 3 , Al(OH) 3 , or basaluminite—stable phases that limit their bioavailability and extractability under neutral pH [ 12 ,  26 ]. Some studies have shown that pH levels below 3 or the addition of reducing agents are needed to release recoverable metal forms. For example, Piñon-Flores et al. [ 18 ] reported that under acidic conditions, Mn and As could be released via dissolution or reduction pathways. However, such processes also pose risks of secondary environmental contamination.

Although Brunauer–Emmett–Teller analysis has revealed that certain CMDS samples possess relatively large specific surface areas (> 30 m 2  g − 1 ) and suitable pore diameters and volumes for adsorption applications [ 63 ], these characteristics do not guarantee easy metal recovery. In fact, highly amorphous and co-precipitated structures may hinder selective extraction. Lee et al. [ 36 ] further demonstrated that even after modification with PU coating, the primary components of CMDS remained chemically stable, indicating that in-situ metal recovery is challenging and that CMDS is more suitable for indirect applications rather than direct metal extraction. It is worth noting, however, that pretreatment can alter the iron mineral phases in the sludge, enabling broader application scenarios. For example, Liang et al. [ 198 ] used a hydrothermal method to convert Fe-rich sludge into KFeS 2  whiskers, achieving efficient removal of Zn and Ni.

In summary, although CMDS contains high concentrations of valuable elements, these are mostly present in stable, poorly soluble mineral forms. Extracting them often requires energy-intensive methods such as strong acid or high-temperature treatment, which also carry environmental risks. Therefore, the development of “indirect utilization” models—such as using CMDS as adsorbents, catalysts, or stabilizers—may be more appropriate than direct metal recovery.

sections.heading: Mobility of hazardous elements
paragraphs: CMDS contains heavy metals (e.g., Fe, Mn, As, Al) predominantly in oxide forms. Upon resource utilization, these elements may be remobilized through microbial redox processes [ 199 ]. Under anaerobic and acidic conditions, iron-reducing microorganisms such as  Ferroplasma acidiphilum  can reduce Fe(III) to the more soluble Fe(II) via dissimilatory iron reduction, significantly increasing Fe mobility in aqueous environments [ 200 ,  201 ].

Certain dissimilatory bacteria, such as iron- and nitrate-reducing species, can reduce adsorbed As(V) in CMDS to the more toxic and mobile As(III), promoting its release from solid to aqueous phases [ 202 ,  203 ]. Moreover, studies have shown that sulfate-reducing bacteria, Methanogenic archaea, and a novel bacterial strain SM-1 can methylate solid-phase arsenic into organic species such as dimethylarsinic acid and trimethylarsine oxide, and even volatilize it as trimethylarsine, significantly enhancing arsenic mobility and bioavailability [ 204 ,  205 ].

Low-molecular-weight organic acids (e.g., citric and oxalic acid) produced by microbial metabolism can also complex with aluminum, increasing its mobility in aquatic systems—a process widely observed in acidic soils [ 206 ]. Consequently, CMDS, under microbial influence, may release heavy metals and other contaminants, with their toxicity potentially further enhanced, posing elevated ecological risks. Avoiding such risks is a crucial consideration in the resource utilization of CMDS.

This study recommends that, in addition to evaluating the key performance metrics of CMDS-based products, leaching tests should be conducted according to the intended application scenarios to assess heavy metal mobility (Table  4 ). Such assessments are essential to effectively mitigate heavy metal risks.

sections.heading: Opportunities and challenges in the resource utilization of CMDS
paragraphs: This study discusses the resource utilization potential of CMDS. Research has shown that CMDS, due to its high metal content—particularly iron—is considered a valuable resource. The utilization pathways of CMDS include serving as a heavy metal adsorbent for wastewater purification, acting as a catalyst in AOPs to degrade organic pollutants, stabilizing heavy metals in soil to prevent further contamination, and functioning as a liner material in landfills. The advantages and disadvantages of these application scenarios are summarized in Table  5 . From the perspective of CMDS pretreatment for resource utilization, five main categories can be identified: direct use or use after sieving; use after ambient or low-temperature drying; use after high-temperature drying and sieving; conversion into special materials at low temperatures; and pH-controlled precipitation methods (Fig.  5 ; Table  6 ). Each of these pretreatment approaches has demonstrated certain degrees of applicability, yet all face some limitations at the current stage. Moving forward, a key factor in identifying viable commercial applications will be the ability to appropriately address both the opportunities and challenges associated with CMDS resource utilization.
